lead: A three-phase AC voltage controller sets the RMS voltage of a three-phase load by delaying thyristor firing, for heaters, furnaces and motor soft starters. The connection decides everything: with a neutral the phases are independent, but in a three-wire star the load currents must add to zero and the phases interact. The exam asks for the configurations and for the firing ranges and RMS output of the three-wire star.
prereq: You need: the single-phase controller from AC voltage controllers: phase and on-off control, and three-phase line and phase quantities.

blocks.text: Each line or branch gets two antiparallel SCRs, or a TRIAC at low power. V<sub>L</sub> is the RMS line voltage and V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>/√3 the RMS supply phase voltage.

items: Star load with neutral (four-wire): three independent single-phase controllers; α runs from 0° to 180° and the single-phase formula applies per phase. The neutral carries the triplen harmonics (3rd, 9th, …) of all three phases, which add.
Three-wire star, fully controlled: six SCRs in the lines, no neutral. The phases interact and the range for a resistive load is 0° to 150°. The usual circuit for soft starters.

Three-wire star, half-controlled: an SCR and a diode in antiparallel in each line. Only three gate circuits, but the halves differ, so even harmonics appear; the range is 0° to 210°. Small heaters only.

Delta load, controllers inside the delta: an SCR pair in series with each branch. Each branch is a single-phase controller on the line voltage (0° to 180°), and the SCRs carry only the branch current.
Delta load, controllers in the lines: behaves like the three-wire star, with the same 0° to 150° range.

sections.h3: Three-wire star with a resistive load

blocks.text: The SCRs are fired 60° apart in the order T1 (line a, positive), T2 (c, negative), T3 (b, positive), T4 (a, negative), T5 (c, positive), T6 (b, negative), with α measured from the zero crossing of phase a. Current needs two SCRs in different lines, so each SCR gets a second pulse 60° after its first (double pulsing); above α = 60° its partner would otherwise already be off.

blocks.where: V<sub>o</sub> is the RMS voltage across each load resistor and α is in radians. The forms meet at 60° (0.841 V<sub>ph</sub>) and 90° (0.541 V<sub>ph</sub>) and give zero at 150°.

blocks.text: Why zero at 150°? T1 conducts with T6 through v<sub>ab</sub> or with T2 through v<sub>ac</sub>. At α = 150° the pair T1, T6 is fired just as v<sub>ab</sub> reaches zero, and the pair T1, T2 just as v<sub>ac</sub> does, so no current can start.

sections.h3: Harmonics, the delta connection and uses

blocks.text: With equal firing and a balanced load the line currents contain harmonics of order 6k ± 1: 5th, 7th, 11th, 13th. Triplens are in phase in all three lines, and three-wire line currents must add to zero, so there are none. In the four-wire star the triplens add in the neutral, which carries a large current near α = 90°.
Inside a delta each branch current has its own 3rd harmonic, but the line current is the difference of two branch currents, so the triplens cancel in the lines and circulate round the delta.

A soft starter begins at a large α (low voltage) and reduces α so the motor voltage ramps up with the current held at a set limit. Unequal firing angles are avoided: they unbalance the load and add negative-sequence current that heats a motor.

examples.question: A 415 V, 50 Hz, three-phase supply feeds a star-connected resistive load of 10 Ω per phase through a fully controlled three-wire controller. Find the RMS load phase voltage, the line current and the total power at (a) α = 60°, (b) α = 120°.
examples.answer: (a) 201.4 V, 20.14 A, 12.17 kW. (b) 49.8 V, 4.98 A, 745 W. With a neutral, 120° would give 239.6 × 0.442 = 105.9 V by the single-phase formula.

examples.question: Three 30 Ω resistors in delta are each fed through their own SCR pair inside the delta from a 415 V, 50 Hz supply. At α = 90°, find the branch voltage and current, the total power, and compare the line current with √3 times the branch current.
steps: Each branch is a single-phase controller on the 415 V line voltage. At α = 90° the bracket is 0.5, so V<sub>branch</sub> = 415 × √0.5 = 293.4 V.

Sine currents would give a line current of √3 × 9.78 = 16.9 A. But the line current is the difference of two branch currents, whose equal 3rd harmonics cancel; subtracting the two chopped waveforms point by point and taking the RMS gives 14.9 A.
examples.answer: V<sub>branch</sub> = 293.4 V, I<sub>branch</sub> = 9.78 A, P = 8.61 kW, line current 14.9 A, which is 1.53 times the branch current, not 1.73. At α = 0° the currents are sines and the ratio is √3 (13.83 A and 23.96 A).

traps: Applying the single-phase formula to one phase of a three-wire star. At α = 120° it gives 105.9 V on 415 V instead of the correct 49.8 V.
Writing 180° as the zero-output angle of a three-wire star. It is 150°; 180° holds for the four-wire star and for controllers inside a delta.
Forgetting double pulsing. With single short pulses the controller cannot work above α = 60°, because two SCRs in different lines must be on together.
Expecting triplen harmonics in the line currents of a balanced three-wire load. They circulate inside a delta or flow in a neutral, never in the three lines alone.

quiz.q: List the configurations of a three-phase AC voltage controller.
quiz.a: Star with neutral (four-wire), three-wire star fully controlled (six SCRs), three-wire star half-controlled (three SCRs and three diodes), delta with controllers inside the branches, and delta with controllers in the lines.

quiz.q: For a three-wire star resistive load, state the three ranges of α and how many SCRs conduct in each.
quiz.a: 0° to 60°: three and two in turn. 60° to 90°: two. 90° to 150°: two, then none. The output is zero from 150°.

quiz.q: Why must each SCR of a three-wire controller get a second pulse 60° after the first?
quiz.a: Current needs one SCR in each of two lines. When α > 60°, the SCR fired 60° earlier has already turned off, so it must be fired again together with the new one; the second pulse does that.

quiz.q: A 400 V supply feeds a 20 Ω per phase star load through a three-wire controller at α = 90°. Find V<sub>o</sub>, I and P.
Thirty-ohm branches inside a delta are fed through SCR pairs from 415 V at α = 0°. Find the branch current, line current and power.
quiz.a: The branches get the full line voltage: I<sub>branch</sub> = 415/30 = 13.83 A. The currents are sines, so the line current is √3 × 13.83 = 23.96 A. P = 3 × 415²/30 = 17.22 kW.

quiz.q: In a three-wire star controller one line is fired at α = 60° and another at 120°. What happens to the load?
quiz.a: The phase voltages and currents become unequal and the floating star point moves. The line currents still add to zero, so they carry no zero-sequence part, but the unbalance adds negative-sequence current, which heats a motor, and lets 3rd-harmonic current into the lines.

beyond: Not for the exam. Many soft starters control only two of the three lines, and an inside-delta soft starter carries only 58 % of the line current. Thyristor-switched capacitors use the same SCR pairs, fired when the supply voltage equals the capacitor voltage. Search for "soft starter current limit", "inside delta soft starter" and "thyristor switched capacitor".

figure.caption: RMS output of a three-wire star controller with a resistive load, as a fraction of the supply phase voltage. It falls to zero at 150°; the dashed curve is one phase with a neutral, which reaches zero only at 180°.

spec.aria: Plot of output ratio against firing angle with three shaded ranges, marked at 60 degrees (0.841) and 120 degrees (0.208), and a dashed single-phase curve.
